hops.afterHeading: What the bulb sends, and the puzzle
hops.title: The myth of the tiny human olfactory bulb
hops.text: In 1879 French anatomist Paul Broca sorted mammals into those driven mainly by smell and a minority less guided by it. He included semiaquatic carnivores, cetaceans (describing reduced olfactory structures in whales and absent ones in dolphins), and primates including humans, whose large frontal lobes, he argued, let them choose how to respond to odors. His grouping used no smell test, yet the belief that humans smell poorly persisted over a century. In 2008, Yale researchers estimated an average of 5,568 glomeruli per human bulb from sampled sections. Divided by the genomic estimate of about 350 intact receptor types they used, that ratio of totals is roughly 16 to one.

sources.citation: McGann JP (2017) Poor human olfaction is a 19th-century myth. Science 356(6338):eaam7263.
Maresh A, Rodriguez Gil D, Whitman MC, Greer CA (2008) Principles of glomerular organization in the human olfactory bulb: implications for odor processing. PLoS ONE 3(7):e2640.

hops.title: How a fruit fly's smell wiring improved computer search
hops.text: Hashing-based methods that find similar photos or documents, such as conventional locality-sensitive hashing, compress each item into a short code. In 2017 Sanjoy Dasgupta, Charles Stevens and Saket Navlakha pointed out that the fruit fly's smell circuit does the opposite. In their model, signals from about 50 odor channels spread out, largely at random, onto about 2,000 cells, and only the most active 5 percent are kept as the odor's tag. Similar odors end up with overlapping tags. Turned into a search algorithm on three standard benchmarks, this expand-and-sparsify trick beat conventional locality-sensitive hashing. The piriform model in this lesson uses a similar logic: scattered wiring plus a threshold.

sources.citation: Dasgupta S, Stevens CF, Navlakha S (2017) A neural algorithm for a fundamental computing problem. Science 358(6364):793-796.
Salk Institute (2017) Fruit fly brains inform search engines of the future. News release.

image.caption: A fly's smell circuit inspired a search algorithm that beat conventional locality-sensitive hashing on three benchmark datasets.

hops.afterHeading: Smell loss in people, and a learned odour map
hops.title: When 'no smell' candle reviews tracked COVID-19 cases
hops.text: During the pandemic, Amazon shoppers kept posting reviews saying their scented candles had no smell. People are often unaware of their own smell loss, so the political scientist Nick Beauchamp asked whether those complaints tracked COVID-19. He collected 9,837 reviews of four best-selling Yankee Candles from late 2018 to late 2021 and adjusted for the rise in 'no smell' reviews that appears every winter. In his model, each extra 100,000 weekly U.S. cases was linked to a rise of about a quarter of a percentage point in the next week's share of no-smell reviews. Perfume reviews showed a weaker hint of the same pattern. Pre-pandemic flu showed none.

sources.citation: Beauchamp N (2022) 'This Candle Has No Smell': detecting the effect of COVID anosmia on Amazon reviews using Bayesian vector autoregression. Proceedings of the International AAAI Conference on Web and Social Media 16(1):1363-1367.

audio.title: Three surprises in how brains smell
audio.transcript:
Smell has a reputation as the quiet sense, the one humans supposedly traded away for big brains. Look at the wiring from the nose to the cortex, though, and it keeps upending what the experts assumed. Here are three true stories.

First, the myth. In eighteen seventy-nine, the French anatomist Paul Broca grouped humans with a small set of mammals he thought were not driven mainly by smell. Alongside semiaquatic carnivores, he included whales, describing their olfactory structures as reduced, and dolphins, which he said lacked them. Humans were there for a different reason: he argued that our bulbs had shrunk, relative to the brain, as our frontal lobes grew large, and that free will, not smell, steered our behavior. His grouping was not based on any test of smell, yet the belief that humans have a poor sense of smell stuck for more than a century. In two thousand and eight, researchers at Yale used sampled tissue sections to estimate how many glomeruli sit in human bulbs. In a mouse, across roughly eleven hundred receptor types, neurons carrying a given type typically converge on two glomeruli per bulb. The human bulbs in the study averaged an estimated five thousand five hundred and sixty-eight glomeruli each. Dividing that average by the genomic estimate of about three hundred and fifty intact receptor types the study used gives a ratio of totals of roughly sixteen to one. Then, a study published online in twenty nineteen reported something stranger: two healthy young left-handed women with no apparent olfactory bulbs on M R I. Both scored in the normal range on the standardized Sniffin' Sticks smell test and showed odor-evoked activity in piriform cortex similar in extent to that of controls, though the second woman scored below the local control mean on the full University of Pennsylvania Smell Identification Test. In a public brain-scan database of one thousand one hundred and thirteen people, the team found three women who could identify odors despite having no clearly defined olfactory bulbs on M R I, with a fourth possible case. As of that report, nobody knew how they manage it.

Second, a fear that needs no training. Untrained laboratory mice avoid the part of a chamber scented with T M T, a volatile compound whose reported presence in fox droppings remains disputed, and they move less while it is there. The same mice are drawn toward two-phenylethanol, a compound in rose oil. In twenty fourteen, Cory Root, Richard Axel and their colleagues used light to silence the bulb's axons in the cortical amygdala. That is the target where the output of a single glomerulus lands in tidy, repeatable patches instead of scattering. With the light on, the mice avoided T M T far less, and their attraction to the rose compound disappeared. When the light went off, both responses came back. So the patchy, stereotyped pathway takes part in odor responses that the mice never had to learn.

Third, the rhythm of a single breath. In nineteen eighty-three, David Laing tested twenty-one volunteers and found that one natural sniff, lasting about zero point four seconds, told them as much about whether an odor was there and how strong it was as seven or more sniffs. Twenty years later, Naoshige Uchida and Zachary Mainen showed that rats can tell closely overlapping odor mixtures apart within a single sniff, in under two hundred milliseconds. Some mammals even sniff underwater. In two thousand and six, Kenneth Catania found that star-nosed moles and American water shrews blow tiny air bubbles onto underwater objects or scent trails, then suck the same bubbles back into their noses to smell them.
